More than 1,300 people are missing in Nepal and Tibet, including 47 Americans, after a glacial collapse caused catastrophic floods, with video showing mud sweeping through entire communities. Drone footage in Nepal showed roads destroyed and buildings buried by thundering water the color of wet cement. Nepalese authorities ramped up operations in the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet is not a one-off. The Lhende Khola river system has now flooded twice in just 14 months and the increasingly unstable Himalayan ice system threatens communities, infrastructure and water supplies across one of the world’s most densely populated regions. The region saw similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged.

Après avoir regardé différentes images des zones inondées, je suis tombé sur une vidéo qui prétend montrer l'endroit où tout aurait commencé. Selon ceux qui la diffusent, la catastrophe n'aurait rien à voir avec le réchauffement climatique, un glissement de terrain ou un glacier. Au tout début de la vidéo, on distingue ce qui ressemble à un avion militaire, présenté comme un F-16, ainsi qu'une explosion près d'un barrage. Certains internautes affirment qu'une bombe aurait été larguée et que le barrage aurait été volontairement détruit, provoquant les inondations que l'on connaît.D'autres vont encore plus loin et avancent que cela pourrait être lié au refus du Premier ministre népalais de collaborer avec ce qu'ils appellent « l'État profond mondial ». Mais ces affirmations sont-elles vérifiables ? L'avion est-il réellement un F-16 ? L'explosion a-t-elle véritablement eu lieu au Népal ? Et surtout, cette séquence montre-t-elle réellement l'origine des inondations ? Regardez attentivement le début de la vidéo et faites-vous votre propre opinion.

Nepal has been hit by a catastrophic flash flood disaster, beginning on 26 August 2026, particularly along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors. 🇳🇵 What happened? The flooding was not simply ordinary monsoon flooding. A sudden ice/rock avalanche and collapse in the Himalayan region near Tibet caused a huge surge of water, mud, rocks and debris into the Bhote Koshi River. The resulting flash flood swept through villages and infrastructure with very little warning.  The worst-affected areas include Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan, with impacts also reported in Gorkha and Tanahun.  🕯️ Deaths and missing people The situation has continued to worsen as rescue teams recover bodies and update missing-person lists. As of 29–30 August, reports indicate more than 600 people have died in Nepal, with thousands still missing across Nepal and Tibet. AP reported 669 deaths in Nepal and nearly 3,000 people still missing as of August 30.  Many of the missing include foreign nationals, tourists, pilgrims and workers. 🚨 Rescue operation Nepalese security forces, helicopters and emergency teams are continuing search-and-rescue operations. More than 3,700 people have reportedly been rescued, while difficult mountain terrain, damaged roads and unstable conditions are making the operation extremely difficult.  A temporary lake formed near the disaster area also created fears of another flood, although the immediate risk has reportedly decreased as the lake has begun draining.  💔 Damage The floods have destroyed or severely damaged: Homes and entire villages Roads and bridges Hydropower plants Electricity infrastructure Border/trade infrastructure Health facilities Tourist and pilgrimage routes Nepal's government estimates that rebuilding could cost approximately US$4–5 billion.  The Nepal Ministry of Foreign Affairs has also been publishing official updates on the disaster and missing foreign nationals.
